Every assignment that fits splits into two groups that give opposite answers, so the examples do not determine the new task. The predictions below take one of the two outcomes; there is about a 50% chance they are all correct.

**Which feature each Y component picks** (each matches every example):
- **Y1** is bit 1. In X3-Y1-Z2, button 3 appears exactly when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli; otherwise it is 0.
- **Y2** is bit 3. In X6-Y2-Z1, button 2 appears exactly when bit 3 is 1 in both; otherwise it is 3. In X1-Y2-Z4, button 1 appears exactly when exactly one bit 3 is 1; otherwise it is 0. In X5-Y2-Z2, button 0 appears exactly when neither bit 3 is 1; otherwise it is 3.
- **Y3** is bit 4. In X5-Y3-Z1, button 2 appears exactly when neither bit 4 is 1; otherwise it is 3. In X4-Y3-Z3, button 2 appears when the two bit-4 values are the same and 0 when they differ.

**Possible meanings for the X and Z components:**
- **X3 and X6** are "both" and "not both" in some order.
  - The order is tied to X5 through Z1 and Z2.
  - If X5 means "neither": Z1 gives 2 when true, Z2 gives 0 when true, X6 means "both" and X3 means "not both".
  - If X5 means "at least one": Z1 gives 3 when true, Z2 gives 3 when true, X6 means "not both" and X3 means "both".
- **X1 and X4** are "exactly one" and "same" in some order.
  - If X1 means "exactly one", Z4 gives 1 when true and 0 when false.
  - If X1 means "same", Z4 gives 0 when true and 1 when false.
  - Nothing else in the examples constrains this choice.

That gives four consistent assignments in total.

**New task X5-Y1-Z4 (look at bit 1 of both stimuli):**

| X5 means | X1 means | Neither bit 1 is 1 | At least one bit 1 is 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| neither | exactly one | 1 | 0 |
| neither | same | 0 | 1 |
| at least one | exactly one | 0 | 1 |
| at least one | same | 1 | 0 |

So there are two outcomes, each supported by two assignments. The examples cannot decide between them.

Inputs where neither bit 1 is 1: 1, 8, 10, 12, 14. All other inputs have at least one bit 1 equal to 1.

I chose the outcome where "neither bit 1 is 1" gives button 1 and everything else gives button 0.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
